Lesson 12.1

DLL Identity and Search Order

The previous chapter treated the game as a running process. A process dump or module snapshot can list its DLLs, but a familiar DLL name alone does not prove which file supplied the code. Module identity is the next layer of evidence. We will follow that identity through loading and API resolution, then ask which privileges protect the kernel boundary and how a physical-memory capture relates to a process address. At each stage, the practical question is the same: what did the tool actually observe and trust?

A module name is not a full identity

Section titled “A module name is not a full identity”

A game may report that it loaded opengl32.dll, zlib1.dll, or another familiar name. The name alone does not say which file supplied the bytes. The full path, file hash, signer, architecture, and loaded range provide stronger identity.

TL;DR: A DLL name is a clue; path, build, hash, architecture, and loaded range make the observation specific.

That matters for debugging as well as defense. Loading the wrong version of a legitimate DLL can cause missing exports, crashes, changed structure layouts, or code patterns that no longer match the ones this course uses.

The same DLL name can identify different bytes. This step-by-step trace needs JavaScript. Here is the code and where the run ends.

basename = zlib1.dll
read the selected loaded path
record this build fingerprint and architecture
record its loaded range
compare the full identity with the baseline
report which evidence changed

Result: this fixture matches its baseline identity.

Final values: installation = A; basename = zlib1.dll; path = /fixture/A/zlib1.dll; fingerprint = recorded-build-A; architecture = 32-bit; base = 0x1000; end = 0x2000; matches_baseline = true.

Imports begin a dependency graph

Section titled “Imports begin a dependency graph”

The PE import table names DLLs and functions the image expects. The Windows loader must locate suitable DLL files, map them, resolve imported function addresses, and repeat the process for those DLLs’ dependencies.

Alternative: Module loading grows a dependency tree: each imported library can bring its own imports, so the final loaded set is larger than one executable’s list.

The final loaded set can also include modules requested later with LoadLibrary, graphics layers, accessibility tools, capture software, overlays, or optional game components.

The loader owns the transition from a requested dependency name to a mapped, registered module in the process:

A module snapshot observes the published records after these steps. It does not own the mappings and must not treat a snapshot entry as permission to unload one.

Search order is a compatibility and security boundary

Section titled “Search order is a compatibility and security boundary”

When code supplies only a DLL name instead of a full path, Windows follows documented resolution rules. Those rules depend on factors such as packaged-app identity, API sets (virtual DLL names that Windows redirects to whichever real DLL implements them on that build), side-by-side manifests, already loaded modules, the KnownDLLs list (a fixed set of core system DLLs, recorded in the registry, that Windows always loads from the trusted system directory instead of searching for them), safe DLL search mode (a per-process setting that moves the current working directory later in the search order, so a file planted there is less likely to be picked over the real system DLL), the executable directory, system directories, and configured search paths.

Do not reduce that to “Windows always checks this one folder first.” The precise order depends on how the load was requested and the Windows environment.

For the most common case, an unpackaged desktop program that calls LoadLibrary with a bare name while safe DLL search mode is on (the default), Microsoft documents this order:

The first searched folder that contains a file with that name supplies the DLL. Every check above the numbered searches happens before any folder is searched, which is why a planted file cannot stand in for a KnownDLL. With safe DLL search mode off, the current directory moves up to second place, right after the application’s directory; holding it back at fifth place, behind the system directories, is what the setting does. Packaged apps and a few redirection features add steps that the diagram leaves out.

Safer application design uses:

  • supported installation directories with controlled permissions;
  • manifests and supported side-by-side versioning where appropriate;
  • LoadLibraryEx flags that express the intended search scope;
  • absolute paths for application-controlled plug-ins when practical;
  • no writable current-working directory inserted into dependency search.

This lesson observes what actually loaded. It does not place replacement DLLs into candidate folders or redirect the loader.

Take a ToolHelp module snapshot

Section titled “Take a ToolHelp module snapshot”

TH32CS_SNAPMODULE lists modules matching the tool’s native architecture. TH32CS_SNAPMODULE32 also asks a 64-bit inspector to include 32-bit modules. The course uses both because the historical game builds are 32-bit.

Each MODULEENTRY32W includes:

  • modBaseAddr: live module base;
  • modBaseSize: mapped image size;
  • szModule: short module name;
  • szExePath: full file path;
  • the owner PID and module handles used by Windows.

The structure has a fixed layout, and the caller must set dwSize first because that layout’s size differs between 32-bit and 64-bit builds. In the 32-bit build this course uses, it looks like this:

Complete lab source: module_inventory.rs

module_inventory.rs

windows-labs/src/bin/ · Rust, 75 lines

View on GitHub ↗

Show the codeHide the code
#[cfg(windows)]
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    use std::mem::size_of;

    use gha_windows_labs::{OwnedHandle, Process};
    use windows::Win32::{
        Foundation::ERROR_NO_MORE_FILES,
        System::Diagnostics::ToolHelp::{
            CreateToolhelp32Snapshot, MODULEENTRY32W, Module32FirstW, Module32NextW,
            TH32CS_SNAPMODULE, TH32CS_SNAPMODULE32,
        },
    };

    fn wide_text(buffer: &[u16]) -> String {
        let end = buffer
            .iter()
            .position(|unit| *unit == 0)
            .unwrap_or(buffer.len());
        String::from_utf16_lossy(&buffer[..end])
    }

    fn no_more_files(error: &windows::core::Error) -> bool {
        error.code() == ERROR_NO_MORE_FILES.to_hresult()
    }

    let process_name = std::env::args()
        .nth(1)
        .unwrap_or_else(|| "wesnoth.exe".to_owned());
    let process = Process::find(&process_name)?;
    let flags = TH32CS_SNAPMODULE | TH32CS_SNAPMODULE32;
    // SAFETY: the PID is a value and OwnedHandle owns the returned snapshot.
    let snapshot = unsafe { CreateToolhelp32Snapshot(flags, process.id) }?;
    let snapshot = OwnedHandle::from_raw(snapshot)?;
    let mut entry = MODULEENTRY32W {
        dwSize: size_of::<MODULEENTRY32W>() as u32,
        ..Default::default()
    };

    // SAFETY: entry has the required size and remains writable during the call.
    unsafe { Module32FirstW(snapshot.raw(), &mut entry) }?;
    let mut modules = Vec::new();
    loop {
        modules.push((
            entry.modBaseAddr as usize,
            entry.modBaseSize as usize,
            wide_text(&entry.szModule),
            wide_text(&entry.szExePath),
        ));
        // SAFETY: entry remains a correctly sized writable output structure.
        match unsafe { Module32NextW(snapshot.raw(), &mut entry) } {
            Ok(()) => {}
            Err(error) if no_more_files(&error) => break,
            Err(error) => return Err(error.into()),
        }
    }

    modules.sort_unstable_by_key(|(base, _, _, _)| *base);
    println!(
        "{} (PID {}) loaded {} module(s)",
        process.name,
        process.id,
        modules.len()
    );
    for (base, size, name, file) in modules {
        println!("  {base:#010x}  {size:#010x}  {name}");
        println!("              {file}");
    }
    println!("The snapshot was read-only; no loader state was changed.");
    Ok(())
}

#[cfg(not(windows))]
fn main() {
    eprintln!("This read-only module inventory must run on Windows.");
}

Run a clean baseline

Section titled “Run a clean baseline”
Windows VM

Start a fresh local game without optional overlays or mod loaders:

Capture the result again after entering a match. Some games delay-load graphics, audio, or networking components, so a later list may legitimately be longer.

Repeat the experiment for AssaultCube and Urban Terror:

Turn the list into a baseline

Section titled “Turn the list into a baseline”

An approved baseline describes each non-system module with:

  • full canonical path;
  • SHA-256 hash from the integrity-manifest lesson;
  • file size and version;
  • expected publisher or project source;
  • why and when the game loads it;
  • which exact game build the entry belongs to.

A different module is not automatically malicious. It may be a graphics capture layer, accessibility tool, language pack, supported mod, or updated dependency. Investigate before removing anything.

Snapshot limitations

Section titled “Snapshot limitations”

The module list is a moment-in-time view. A DLL may load or unload immediately afterward. A module manually mapped without normal loader registration may not appear in the ToolHelp loader list. A protected or cross-architecture target may restrict enumeration.

A DLL that loads and unloads between two snapshots appears in neither list, even though its code ran inside the game:

Narration: Two clean snapshots can miss a DLL that ran and unloaded between them. Snapshot absence is therefore weaker than a complete history of loads.

Each of these sources sees module loading from a different place, so each one covers something another misses:

  • ToolHelp module list: the modules the loader has registered, at one instant;
  • ETW image-load events: every image mapping and unmapping over time, including DLLs that came and went between snapshots;
  • file hashes and signatures: which bytes are on disk, and who signed them;
  • the process memory map: every committed region, including executable memory that no module in the list accounts for;
  • the PE import table: which DLLs the executable declares it needs before it runs;
  • debugger module events: load and unload notifications as they happen.

Keep defensive observation separate from loader manipulation

Section titled “Keep defensive observation separate from loader manipulation”

The course does not hide modules, unlink loader entries, overwrite an existing module, or exploit search-order mistakes. Those actions corrupt the loader records that this chapter’s tools read, and that debuggers and crash reporters rely on too.

The complete inventory is module_inventory.rs. Combine its paths with integrity_manifest.rs for a repeatable baseline.

References: dynamic-link library search order, ToolHelp snapshots, and MODULEENTRY32W.

Lesson 12.2

DLL Loading and the Loader Lock

Loading a DLL is a coordinated operation

Section titled “Loading a DLL is a coordinated operation”

When Windows loads a DLL, it does more than copy bytes. The loader maps PE sections, applies relocations when needed, resolves imports, prepares thread-local storage, updates module bookkeeping, and calls initialization entry points.

Other threads must not observe a half-initialized module. Windows serializes important parts of loading with a process-wide synchronization mechanism commonly called the loader lock.

That creates a special rule: Windows calls DllMain while the loader lock is held.

Initialization is a dependency-order problem

Section titled “Initialization is a dependency-order problem”

Each initialization step depends on other services already being ready. Import resolution depends on module loading; logging may depend on files, locks, or other DLLs; a hook may depend on the target module and worker state. DllMain runs inside the mechanism that is still satisfying some of those dependencies.

Alternative: Initialization is a dependency ladder: logging, workers, and hooks belong on steps whose supporting services are already ready.

Draw the order before writing startup code:

The arrows are dependency claims: a step may begin only after the step above it has completed.

Shutdown should reverse ownership, not merely reverse the list of function calls:

An explicit lifecycle makes partially initialized states visible. If verification fails before a patch is installed, cleanup should not pretend the patch exists.

What DllMain notifications mean

Section titled “What DllMain notifications mean”

The entry point can receive reasons such as:

  • DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH: the DLL is being attached to the process;
  • DLL_THREAD_ATTACH: a new thread is being announced to DLLs;
  • DLL_THREAD_DETACH: a thread is ending;
  • DLL_PROCESS_DETACH: the DLL or process is being unloaded.

These are loader notifications, not general application events. The code is running in the context of whichever thread caused the load or unload, and notifications are serialized.

Why ordinary-looking work can deadlock

Section titled “Why ordinary-looking work can deadlock”

Imagine two locks:

Neither thread can continue. The dangerous second lock may be hidden inside a function that loads a DLL, initializes COM, sends a blocking cross-thread message, starts complex runtime work, or waits for another thread.

The version that catches most game tools is subtler, because you never write the second lock yourself:

CreateThread returns success, so nothing appears to have gone wrong. The new thread then blocks before executing a single line of your code, and the wait never finishes. This is precisely why the shutdown sequence above joins worker threads outside the loader lock, and why starting real work belongs in an explicit start() that the host calls once loading has completed.

That is why DllMain should not:

  • load another DLL;
  • initialize COM;
  • create a window or call complex User32/Shell APIs;
  • wait for a worker thread;
  • acquire a lock also used by normal game code;
  • parse configuration, scan memory, install hooks, or run a hotkey loop;
  • perform heavy allocation or logging whose dependencies are unclear.

“It worked on my machine” does not prove the lock ordering is safe. Deadlocks depend on timing.

A deadlock needs a cycle of waits. Write each lock edge as “while holding A, this path may wait for B.” If another path can hold B and wait for A, no timeout makes the ordering correct. Remove the wait from the loader callback or establish one global lock order that every path follows.

The course entry point stays tiny

Section titled “The course entry point stays tiny”

The course DLL does one documented optimization during process attach: it disables per-thread attach/detach notifications that the library does not use.

It does not start the game lab, read memory, scan modules, or wait.

Stage two begins after loading finishes

Section titled “Stage two begins after loading finishes”

The DLL exports a separate function named gha_start. The injector waits for its LoadLibraryW thread to finish first. Only then does it call gha_start, after the initial loader work has returned.

TL;DR: Begin the DLL’s real work only after loading returns, using an explicit entry point with its own result.

Return from the loader callback before waiting. This step-by-step trace needs JavaScript. Here is the code and where the run ends.

Windows maps sections and resolves imports
DllMain runs while the loader lock is held
choose whether the callback waits for a worker
return to release the loader lock
start normal work outside the callback
report progress or a circular wait

Result: ordinary work starts after loader initialization.

Final values: start = outside; loader_lock = released; callback_waits = false; worker = running.

The exported function uses the Windows thread-procedure ABI because the course injector calls it as a separate thread entry:

OnceLock prevents duplicate startup. AtomicBool lets the exported stop function ask the worker loop to finish without blocking inside DllMain.

Separate “request stop” from “wait until stopped”

Section titled “Separate “request stop” from “wait until stopped””

The stop export sets a flag and returns:

The worker notices the flag, leaves its loop, releases any pressed input, and drops owned patches so their original bytes are restored. A loader callback should not wait for that worker while holding the loader lock.

Narration: A stop flag can be set quickly, but waiting for the worker inside a loader callback can trap both sides behind the loader lock.

Why creating a thread in DllMain is still the wrong design here

Section titled “Why creating a thread in DllMain is still the wrong design here”

You may see examples that call CreateThread directly from DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH. The new thread cannot safely finish DLL-dependent initialization until loader notifications are complete. Waiting for it inside DllMain can deadlock, and returning immediately creates a fragile ordering problem.

The explicit gha_start contract is easier to reason about and test:

The original loader callback starts a worker and installs hooks during DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH. That puts initialization under the loader lock, where a worker that needs DLL loading can deadlock.

Move that work to an explicit startup boundary. The injector waits for loading to finish, then calls gha_start; its result reports whether course initialization succeeded.

Improved code

Show the diff

Takeaway: finish loader notification before starting work that may depend on other DLLs.

Why this version?

Section titled “Why this version?”

The boundary is visible. A failure in LoadLibraryW is different from a failure in course initialization, and each stage returns its own result.

Test the lifecycle, not just startup

Section titled “Test the lifecycle, not just startup”

For each exact game DLL profile:

  1. inject the exact 32-bit build;
  2. verify gha_start returns zero;
  3. enable one lab feature;
  4. press End or call gha_stop;
  5. confirm patches restore and input is released;
  6. close the game normally;
  7. repeat to catch one-run initialization assumptions.

If the game hangs while loading or unloading, inspect lock order and work performed by entry points before adding timeouts. A timeout hides a deadlock; it does not repair one.

The complete entry-point implementation is dll.rs, and the two-stage caller is injector.rs.

//! DLL entry points and the small hotkey worker used by the course labs.

#![cfg(target_arch = "x86")]

use std::{
    ffi::c_void,
    path::Path,
    sync::{
        OnceLock,
        atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering},
    },
    thread,
    time::Duration,
};

use anyhow::{Context, Result};
use windows::Win32::{
    Foundation::{HINSTANCE, HMODULE},
    System::{LibraryLoader::DisableThreadLibraryCalls, SystemServices::DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH},
    UI::Input::KeyboardAndMouse::{GetAsyncKeyState, VK_END, VK_F1, VK_F2, VK_F3, VK_F4, VK_F5},
};
use windows::core::BOOL;

use super::{
    LocalPatch, OPENGL_CHAMS, OPENGL_OFF, OPENGL_WALLHACK, TARGET_UNDER_CROSSHAIR,
    assaultcube_aim_once, assaultcube_update_esp, enable_assaultcube_no_recoil,
    enable_assaultcube_show_all_radar, enable_wesnoth_map_reveal, install_assaultcube_esp_hook,
    install_assaultcube_trigger_hook, install_urban_terror_memory_wallhook,
    install_urban_terror_opengl_hook, install_wesnoth_stat_hook, install_wesnoth_terrain_hook,
    run_flare_farming_bot, run_wyrmsun_macro, send_left_mouse, set_urban_terror_opengl_mode,
    write_wesnoth_gold,
};

static STARTED: OnceLock<()> = OnceLock::new();
static STOP: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false);

fn pressed_once(virtual_key: i32) -> bool {
    // SAFETY: GetAsyncKeyState accepts any virtual-key integer and returns a
    // value. The low bit means the key was pressed since the previous query.
    unsafe { GetAsyncKeyState(virtual_key) & 1 != 0 }
}

fn toggle(
    slot: &mut Option<LocalPatch>,
    install: impl FnOnce() -> Result<LocalPatch>,
) -> Result<()> {
    if let Some(mut patch) = slot.take() {
        patch.restore()?;
    } else {
        *slot = Some(install()?);
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn current_process_name() -> Result<String> {
    let executable = std::env::current_exe().context("Windows did not report the game path")?;
    let name = Path::new(&executable)
        .file_name()
        .context("the game path has no file name")?
        .to_string_lossy()
        .into_owned();
    Ok(name)
}

fn run_assaultcube() -> Result<()> {
    let mut trigger = None;
    let mut no_recoil = None;
    let mut radar = None;
    let mut esp = None;
    let mut aimbot_enabled = false;
    let mut mouse_down = false;

    while !STOP.load(Ordering::Acquire) {
        if pressed_once(VK_F1.0.into()) {
            if trigger.is_some() && mouse_down {
                send_left_mouse(false)?;
                mouse_down = false;
            }
            toggle(&mut trigger, install_assaultcube_trigger_hook)?;
            if trigger.is_none() {
                TARGET_UNDER_CROSSHAIR.store(false, Ordering::Release);
            }
        }
        if pressed_once(VK_F2.0.into()) {
            toggle(&mut no_recoil, enable_assaultcube_no_recoil)?;
        }
        if pressed_once(VK_F3.0.into()) {
            toggle(&mut radar, enable_assaultcube_show_all_radar)?;
        }
        if pressed_once(VK_F4.0.into()) {
            aimbot_enabled = !aimbot_enabled;
        }
        if pressed_once(VK_F5.0.into()) {
            toggle(&mut esp, install_assaultcube_esp_hook)?;
        }

        if aimbot_enabled {
            assaultcube_aim_once()?;
        }
        if esp.is_some() {
            assaultcube_update_esp()?;
        }

        let wants_mouse_down = trigger.is_some() && TARGET_UNDER_CROSSHAIR.load(Ordering::Acquire);
        if wants_mouse_down != mouse_down {
            send_left_mouse(wants_mouse_down)?;
            mouse_down = wants_mouse_down;
        }
        if pressed_once(VK_END.0.into()) {
            break;
        }
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(8));
    }

    if mouse_down {
        send_left_mouse(false)?;
    }
    // Dropping these values restores the original instructions in reverse
    // lexical order after the worker has stopped using them.
    drop(esp);
    drop(radar);
    drop(no_recoil);
    drop(trigger);
    Ok(())
}

fn run_wesnoth() -> Result<()> {
    write_wesnoth_gold(999)?;
    let mut terrain = None;
    let mut stat = None;
    let mut map = None;

    while !STOP.load(Ordering::Acquire) {
        if pressed_once(VK_F1.0.into()) {
            toggle(&mut terrain, install_wesnoth_terrain_hook)?;
        }
        if pressed_once(VK_F2.0.into()) {
            toggle(&mut stat, install_wesnoth_stat_hook)?;
        }
        if pressed_once(VK_F3.0.into()) {
            toggle(&mut map, enable_wesnoth_map_reveal)?;
        }
        if pressed_once(VK_END.0.into()) {
            break;
        }
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(20));
    }
    drop(map);
    drop(stat);
    drop(terrain);
    Ok(())
}

fn run_urban_terror() -> Result<()> {
    let mut memory_wallhook = None;
    let mut opengl_hook = None;
    let mut opengl_mode = OPENGL_OFF;

    while !STOP.load(Ordering::Acquire) {
        if pressed_once(VK_F1.0.into()) {
            toggle(&mut memory_wallhook, install_urban_terror_memory_wallhook)?;
        }
        if pressed_once(VK_F2.0.into()) {
            if opengl_mode == OPENGL_WALLHACK {
                set_urban_terror_opengl_mode(OPENGL_OFF)?;
                drop(opengl_hook.take());
                opengl_mode = OPENGL_OFF;
            } else {
                if opengl_hook.is_none() {
                    opengl_hook = Some(install_urban_terror_opengl_hook(OPENGL_WALLHACK)?);
                }
                set_urban_terror_opengl_mode(OPENGL_WALLHACK)?;
                opengl_mode = OPENGL_WALLHACK;
            }
        }
        if pressed_once(VK_F3.0.into()) {
            if opengl_mode == OPENGL_CHAMS {
                set_urban_terror_opengl_mode(OPENGL_OFF)?;
                drop(opengl_hook.take());
                opengl_mode = OPENGL_OFF;
            } else {
                if opengl_hook.is_none() {
                    opengl_hook = Some(install_urban_terror_opengl_hook(OPENGL_CHAMS)?);
                }
                set_urban_terror_opengl_mode(OPENGL_CHAMS)?;
                opengl_mode = OPENGL_CHAMS;
            }
        }
        if pressed_once(VK_END.0.into()) {
            break;
        }
        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(8));
    }

    set_urban_terror_opengl_mode(OPENGL_OFF)?;
    drop(opengl_hook);
    drop(memory_wallhook);
    Ok(())
}

fn run_lab() -> Result<()> {
    let process = current_process_name()?.to_ascii_lowercase();
    match process.as_str() {
        "wesnoth.exe" => run_wesnoth(),
        "ac_client.exe" => run_assaultcube(),
        "quake3-urt.exe" => run_urban_terror(),
        "flare.exe" => run_flare_farming_bot(&STOP),
        "wyrmsun.exe" => run_wyrmsun_macro(&STOP),
        _ => anyhow::bail!("{process:?} is not a configured course target"),
    }
}

/// Windows calls this under the loader lock. Do only the one documented,
/// loader-safe optimization here; the injector calls `gha_start` afterward.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "system" fn DllMain(instance: HINSTANCE, reason: u32, _reserved: *mut c_void) -> BOOL {
    if reason == DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH {
        // SAFETY: `instance` is the module Windows is currently attaching.
        let _ = unsafe { DisableThreadLibraryCalls(HMODULE(instance.0)) };
    }
    BOOL::from(true)
}

/// Exported with the Windows thread-procedure signature so the injector can
/// call it safely after LoadLibraryW has returned and released the loader lock.
#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "system" fn gha_start(_argument: *mut c_void) -> u32 {
    if STARTED.set(()).is_err() {
        return 1; // already running
    }
    STOP.store(false, Ordering::Release);
    let started = thread::Builder::new()
        .name("gha-tool-worker".into())
        .spawn(|| {
            if let Err(error) = run_lab() {
                eprintln!("game lab stopped: {error:#}");
            }
        });
    if started.is_err() {
        return 2;
    }
    0
}

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub extern "system" fn gha_stop(_argument: *mut c_void) -> u32 {
    STOP.store(true, Ordering::Release);
    0
}

#[cfg(windows)]
mod app {
    use std::{ffi::c_void, os::windows::ffi::OsStrExt, path::Path, time::Duration};

    use anyhow::{Context, Result};
    use gha_windows_labs::{OwnedHandle, Process};
    use windows::{
        Win32::{
            Foundation::{FreeLibrary, HMODULE, WAIT_FAILED, WAIT_OBJECT_0, WAIT_TIMEOUT},
            System::{
                LibraryLoader::{
                    DONT_RESOLVE_DLL_REFERENCES, GetModuleHandleW, GetProcAddress, LoadLibraryExW,
                },
                Memory::{
                    MEM_COMMIT, MEM_RELEASE, MEM_RESERVE, PAGE_READWRITE, VirtualAllocEx,
                    VirtualFreeEx,
                },
                Threading::{
                    CreateRemoteThread, GetExitCodeThread, LPTHREAD_START_ROUTINE,
                    PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD, PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION, PROCESS_VM_OPERATION,
                    PROCESS_VM_READ, PROCESS_VM_WRITE, WaitForSingleObject,
                },
            },
        },
        core::{PCWSTR, s, w},
    };

    const ALLOWED_TARGETS: &[&str] = &[
        "wesnoth.exe",
        "ac_client.exe",
        "Quake3-UrT.exe",
        "flare.exe",
        "wyrmsun.exe",
    ];

    struct RemoteAllocation<'a> {
        process: &'a Process,
        address: *mut c_void,
    }

    impl Drop for RemoteAllocation<'_> {
        fn drop(&mut self) {
            // SAFETY: this allocation belongs to this process and is released once.
            let _ =
                unsafe { VirtualFreeEx(self.process.raw_handle(), self.address, 0, MEM_RELEASE) };
        }
    }

    struct LocalModule(HMODULE);

    impl Drop for LocalModule {
        fn drop(&mut self) {
            // SAFETY: this process owns the reference returned by LoadLibraryExW.
            let _ = unsafe { FreeLibrary(self.0) };
        }
    }

    fn wait_for_thread(thread: &OwnedHandle, description: &str) -> Result<u32> {
        let timeout_ms = u32::try_from(Duration::from_secs(10).as_millis())?;
        // SAFETY: the thread handle remains live for the wait.
        let wait = unsafe { WaitForSingleObject(thread.raw(), timeout_ms) };
        if wait == WAIT_TIMEOUT {
            anyhow::bail!("{description} did not finish within 10 seconds");
        }
        if wait == WAIT_FAILED {
            return Err(windows::core::Error::from_thread().into());
        }
        anyhow::ensure!(wait == WAIT_OBJECT_0, "unexpected wait result: {}", wait.0);

        let mut exit_code = 0_u32;
        // SAFETY: the thread has finished and the output pointer is writable.
        unsafe { GetExitCodeThread(thread.raw(), &mut exit_code) }?;
        Ok(exit_code)
    }

    fn wide_absolute_path(path: &Path) -> Result<Vec<u16>> {
        let absolute = path
            .canonicalize()
            .with_context(|| format!("cannot find DLL at {}", path.display()))?;
        let mut wide: Vec<u16> = absolute.as_os_str().encode_wide().collect();
        wide.push(0); // LoadLibraryW expects a zero-terminated UTF-16 string.
        Ok(wide)
    }

    fn as_bytes(wide: &[u16]) -> &[u8] {
        // SAFETY: a u16 slice is contiguous; its byte view is exactly twice as long.
        unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(wide.as_ptr().cast(), wide.len() * 2) }
    }

    pub fn run() -> Result<()> {
        let mut arguments = std::env::args().skip(1);
        let process_name = arguments
            .next()
            .context("usage: injector <allowed-process.exe> <absolute-or-relative-dll-path>")?;
        let dll_path = arguments.next().context("missing DLL path")?;

        anyhow::ensure!(
            ALLOWED_TARGETS
                .iter()
                .any(|allowed| allowed.eq_ignore_ascii_case(&process_name)),
            "{process_name:?} is not one of the course targets"
        );

        let entry = Process::find(&process_name)?;
        let access = PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD
            | PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION
            | PROCESS_VM_OPERATION
            | PROCESS_VM_READ
            | PROCESS_VM_WRITE;
        let process = Process::open_with_access(entry, access)?;
        anyhow::ensure!(
            process.is_32_bit()?,
            "the course DLLs require a 32-bit target"
        );

        let wide_path = wide_absolute_path(Path::new(&dll_path))?;
        let path_bytes = as_bytes(&wide_path);

        // Reserve and commit readable/writable memory inside the game.
        // SAFETY: the process handle is live; null asks Windows to choose the address.
        let remote_address = unsafe {
            VirtualAllocEx(
                process.raw_handle(),
                None,
                path_bytes.len(),
                MEM_COMMIT | MEM_RESERVE,
                PAGE_READWRITE,
            )
        };
        anyhow::ensure!(!remote_address.is_null(), "VirtualAllocEx failed");
        let remote_path = RemoteAllocation {
            process: &process,
            address: remote_address,
        };
        process.write_exact(remote_path.address as usize, path_bytes)?;

        // kernel32 is already loaded in this injector. Resolve LoadLibraryW there.
        // For the same architecture, this system DLL export is usable by the target.
        // SAFETY: both names are static zero-terminated strings.
        let kernel32 = unsafe { GetModuleHandleW(w!("kernel32.dll")) }?;
        // SAFETY: `kernel32` is live and the exported name is valid ASCII.
        let load_library = unsafe { GetProcAddress(kernel32, s!("LoadLibraryW")) }
            .context("kernel32 did not export LoadLibraryW")?;

        // CreateRemoteThread expects the same address with the thread-procedure type.
        // On 32-bit Windows both signatures use the system ABI and one pointer argument.
        // SAFETY: this 32-bit course injector and target use the Windows system
        // ABI; LoadLibraryW accepts one pointer and its HMODULE result fits u32.
        let thread_start: LPTHREAD_START_ROUTINE = Some(unsafe {
            std::mem::transmute::<
                unsafe extern "system" fn() -> isize,
                unsafe extern "system" fn(*mut c_void) -> u32,
            >(load_library)
        });

        // SAFETY: the start address is LoadLibraryW and its argument points to the
        // zero-terminated UTF-16 path that remains allocated until the thread exits.
        let thread = unsafe {
            CreateRemoteThread(
                process.raw_handle(),
                None,
                0,
                thread_start,
                Some(remote_path.address.cast_const()),
                0,
                None,
            )
        }?;
        let thread = OwnedHandle::from_raw(thread)?;

        let module_handle = wait_for_thread(&thread, "the LoadLibraryW thread")?;
        anyhow::ensure!(module_handle != 0, "LoadLibraryW returned null");

        // Map the same DLL in this injector without running DllMain. That lets
        // us ask Windows where the exported `gha_start` function sits relative
        // to the DLL base. The relative offset is identical in the game even
        // when ASLR chooses a different base address there.
        // SAFETY: `wide_path` is still a zero-terminated UTF-16 path.
        let local_module = unsafe {
            LoadLibraryExW(
                PCWSTR(wide_path.as_ptr()),
                None,
                DONT_RESOLVE_DLL_REFERENCES,
            )
        }
        .context("could not map the DLL locally to find gha_start")?;
        let local_module = LocalModule(local_module);
        // SAFETY: the module is live and the export name is zero-terminated.
        let local_start = unsafe { GetProcAddress(local_module.0, s!("gha_start")) }
            .context("the DLL does not export gha_start")?;
        let local_start_address = local_start as *const () as usize;
        let local_base = local_module.0.0 as usize;
        let start_offset = local_start_address
            .checked_sub(local_base)
            .context("gha_start was below the local DLL base")?;
        let remote_start_address = (module_handle as usize)
            .checked_add(start_offset)
            .context("remote gha_start address overflowed")?;
        // SAFETY: this is the `gha_start` RVA in the same 32-bit DLL image.
        // SAFETY: this address is the verified gha_start RVA in the same
        // 32-bit DLL image, whose export uses LPTHREAD_START_ROUTINE's ABI.
        let remote_start: LPTHREAD_START_ROUTINE = Some(unsafe {
            std::mem::transmute::<usize, unsafe extern "system" fn(*mut c_void) -> u32>(
                remote_start_address,
            )
        });

        // SAFETY: gha_start has the documented LPTHREAD_START_ROUTINE ABI and
        // accepts a null argument. The DLL stays loaded in the target.
        let start_thread = unsafe {
            CreateRemoteThread(process.raw_handle(), None, 0, remote_start, None, 0, None)
        }?;
        let start_thread = OwnedHandle::from_raw(start_thread)?;
        let start_result = wait_for_thread(&start_thread, "the gha_start thread")?;
        anyhow::ensure!(
            start_result == 0,
            "gha_start returned error code {start_result}"
        );

        println!(
            "Injected and started {} in {} (PID {}). Module handle: {module_handle:#010x}",
            Path::new(&dll_path).display(),
            process.name(),
            process.id()
        );
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[cfg(windows)]
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    app::run()
}

    eprintln!("The injector uses Windows APIs and must be built on Windows.");

References: DllMain, dynamic-link library best practices, and preventing hangs.

Lesson 12.3

Dynamic Windows API Resolution

Import tables are not the only way to call an API

Section titled “Import tables are not the only way to call an API”

Normally the Windows loader resolves a program’s imports before main. Sometimes a tool supports several Windows versions and wants to use a newer API only when it exists. Then it can:

  1. obtain a handle to the system DLL;
  2. look up the named export;
  3. convert the address to one proven function-pointer type;
  4. call it or choose a fallback.

This is useful compatibility work. It is not a reason to hide imports or replace well-supported APIs with undocumented ones.

Detect the capability you need

Section titled “Detect the capability you need”

Do not infer one API’s presence only from a Windows version string. Compatibility settings, servicing changes, and alternative implementations can make version checks lie about the capability that matters. Look up the documented export, validate the result, and take the fallback when it is absent.

Presence still does not guarantee that one call will succeed. The handle may lack rights, the buffer may be too small, or the target may exit. Feature detection chooses a code path; normal error handling still applies inside that path.

TL;DR: Finding an optional export chooses a capability path; the chosen call still needs ordinary error handling.

Missing capability is different from a failed call. This step-by-step trace needs JavaScript. Here is the code and where the run ends.

look up the documented export
if absent: choose the labelled fallback
otherwise call the typed function
check its actual return result
record result source and limitations
return a value or an explicit error

Result: successful documented query. Export presence and operation success are separate checks.

Final values: export = present; call = ok; present = true; called = true; source = documented query; result = fixture path; limitation = call can fail despite presence.

Define the contract from documentation and assembly

Section titled “Define the contract from documentation and assembly”

For a known API, the Windows SDK declaration is the primary contract. Static analysis can confirm what the compiled caller does: argument registers, stack space, result checks, and error handling.

Keep the type alias beside the resolver:

The pointer type says more than “address of a function.” It records ABI, argument order, mutability, and result width.

Alternative: A typed function pointer is a delivery contract, naming where arguments go and how results return—not merely an address to jump to.

extern "system" names a different calling convention on each of the two targets this course builds, so the same alias arranges the same four values in two different ways. On 32-bit x86 it means stdcall: the caller pushes the arguments from last to first, so when the function starts they sit just above the return address, one per 4-byte stack slot, and the function removes them itself before returning.

On x86-64, Windows passes the first four integer or pointer arguments in registers, in order, and returns an integer result in EAX, the low 32 bits of RAX:

That is why a “close enough” signature fails in ways that have nothing to do with pointer size. Declare three parameters instead of four, and a 32-bit caller pushes 12 bytes while the function still removes 16 with ret 0x10, leaving the stack pointer 4 bytes away from where the caller expects it. On x86-64 the function reads a fourth argument from R9 anyway, whatever that register happens to hold, and writes the result length through it as if it were a pointer.

Resolve from an already loaded system module

Section titled “Resolve from an already loaded system module”

The resolver starts with kernel32.dll in the current process. It looks up QueryFullProcessImageNameW by its exported name, returns None if that name is absent, and otherwise converts the address to the ABI-checked function type established above. The caller can then choose the fallback rather than calling an unknown address.

The Option is intentional. “Export absent” is a supported compatibility state, not necessarily a fatal error.

Cache the typed result only when module lifetime makes that safe. An address obtained from a module becomes invalid if that module can unload. System modules used for the process lifetime are simpler, but a plug-in resolver should keep module ownership and function-pointer lifetime together.

Call with a retryable buffer

Section titled “Call with a retryable buffer”

Windows text APIs often accept a buffer plus an in/out length. Treat the length as untrusted after every call:

length means two different things on the two sides of the call. Suppose the process is Wesnoth at C:\Games\Wesnoth 1.14.9\wesnoth.exe, a 35-character path:

Use an RAII-owned process handle from the earlier Windows chapters. The dynamic call does not change ownership rules.

Design the fallback before lookup

Section titled “Design the fallback before lookup”

An optional API is useful only if the missing case has a defined behavior:

If the full-path API is unavailable, a ToolHelp module snapshot may supply the main module’s path through MODULEENTRY32W.szExePath. It is a different observation: enumeration can fail across architecture or protection boundaries, and the module can change after the snapshot. Label the source and its limits instead of claiming that every fallback is simply a shorter path.

Narration: A fallback may provide a different kind of observation with different limits. Label its source so later code does not silently assume the stronger API succeeded.

Notice that a failed call does not automatically choose the fallback. The API can exist while the handle, buffer, or target state is invalid. Preserve that difference so compatibility logic does not hide an ordinary error.

Detect bad assumptions

Section titled “Detect bad assumptions”

Test the resolver with:

  • the correct export name;
  • one deliberately misspelled name;
  • 32-bit and 64-bit builds;
  • a closed or insufficient-rights process handle;
  • a buffer whose returned length reaches its bound;
  • an ordinary imported call, then compare results.

Never call an unresolved address. Never replace None with address zero. Never choose a “close enough” function signature because two pointer sizes happen to match.

Why this belongs in reversing

Section titled “Why this belongs in reversing”

When you inspect a game or tool, dynamic resolution explains a common pattern: a string names an API, GetProcAddress returns a pointer, and a later indirect call uses it. Reconstructing that chain turns anonymous control flow into a documented contract.

The responsible end state is clear: one typed resolver, one fallback, visible errors, and no hidden capability. That completes the DLL and API path. The next lesson follows a device request through the driver stack: which kernel component receives it, which device owns the work, and where the result returns.

Lesson 12.4

What an Operating System Kernel Does

The tools so far have asked Windows for something: a handle to a game, a copy of four bytes, a list of loaded modules. Each time, something checked whether the tool was allowed to ask, did the work, and sometimes said no. The kernel is the core of the operating system that coordinates those requests with the processor’s highest operating-system privilege. Ordinary programs go through its controlled services to reach shared resources such as another process’s memory, the disk, the display, or a network device.

This lesson answers four questions. How does the processor keep ordinary programs away from the kernel’s powers? How does a program ask the kernel for something anyway? What does the kernel do with its authority? And why can one kernel bug stop the whole computer, when a bug in a game only ends the game? A four-byte ReadProcessMemory request will carry these questions through the user/kernel boundary. The next lesson reads the exact bits the processor checks and follows the request one layer at a time.

The API layers in the previous lesson showed the route a request takes. Here we examine the authority that makes that route work. After the privilege checks, a crash dump will bring threads, modules, and saved registers back together into one process snapshot. Chapter 12 then follows requests across DLL and device boundaries; Chapter 14 builds on that foundation to explain virtual machines and hardware.

Two modes, enforced by the processor

Section titled “Two modes, enforced by the processor”

The kernel and a game run on the same processor, often on the same core, taking turns many times a second. What stops the game from doing what the kernel does: rewriting another process’s memory, reprogramming the disk controller, or simply never giving the processor back?

A protection check in memory the restricted program can overwrite would not stop it. The restriction has to be enforced beyond that writable memory. The processor checks privilege and memory permissions before carrying out an access.

So the processor tracks a privilege level for the code it is running. It checks privileged instructions and page translations against that level. x86 processors define four levels, numbered 0 to 3 and usually drawn as nested rings, with ring 0 the most privileged. Windows uses two of them:

  • kernel mode, ring 0, for the kernel and drivers;
  • user mode, ring 3, for everything else: games, browsers, debuggers, and every tool in this book.

Lesson 12.5 introduced the two modes as permission levels. The processor records the current level in two bits of one of its registers, which Lesson 12.6 reads in a debugger. What matters here is what the processor refuses to do while the level is 3.

What ring 3 is not allowed to do

Section titled “What ring 3 is not allowed to do”

At ring 3 the processor refuses two kinds of thing.

Privileged instructions. Some instructions only make sense for whoever runs the machine. hlt stops the processor until the next interrupt. cli turns interrupts off, which would silence the timer the kernel relies on to take the processor back. mov cr3, rax switches to a different set of page tables, which selects a process’s whole view of memory. The physical-memory lessons in Chapter 12 will follow those page tables. wrmsr rewrites the processor’s internal settings. At ring 3, each of these raises a general-protection fault instead of running, and the kernel turns the fault into an exception that normally ends the program.

Memory marked for the kernel. Page-table entries carry a user/supervisor bit, bit 2. When it is 0 on a present mapping, a ring-3 access causes a page fault. Windows reserves a system range of virtual addresses for the kernel. In a traditional shared page table, kernel pages can be mapped there alongside a game’s pages, but their supervisor bit still blocks the game. With KVA shadow, the user-mode page table omits most kernel mappings and keeps only the pages needed to enter the kernel; entry code switches to the fuller kernel page table. In either arrangement, a game cannot read or write the kernel’s privileged pages. Lesson 12.6 compares the flag bits of a user page and a kernel page.

Put the two checks together and user-mode code is boxed in. It cannot run the instructions that change privilege or page mappings, and it cannot alter the kernel’s page tables.

A system call is how a program asks

Section titled “A system call is how a program asks”

If ring 3 cannot touch kernel memory or raise its own level, how does ReadProcessMemory ever reach code that can read another process? Through a system call: an instruction that switches the processor to ring 0 and jumps to an address the kernel chose. On x86-64 the instruction is syscall. When the processor executes it, it:

  1. copies the address of the next instruction into rcx and the flags register into r11, so the kernel can come back later;
  2. switches the privilege level to 0;
  3. jumps to an address held in a processor setting that only ring 0 can change. The kernel wrote that address during boot, using wrmsr.

Step 3 is what makes the design safe. A program chooses when to request a service, never an arbitrary kernel instruction to run. The processor enters a kernel-controlled path, which identifies the requested service and checks its untrusted arguments. This is the controlled crossing promised in Chapter 11, now seen from the processor’s side.

TL;DR: A system call enters a kernel-chosen service path; it does not let the caller pick arbitrary privileged instructions to execute.

Follow one call into the kernel and back

Section titled “Follow one call into the kernel and back”

Take a read like the ones in Lesson 6.3: a handle to the game opened with only query and read rights, and a request for 4 bytes at address 0x0050_1000. Here is the whole round trip:

Your tool’s call passes through kernel32.dll and kernelbase.dll, the layers that Lesson 12.5 followed down the stack, to NtReadVirtualMemory in ntdll.dll. That function is only a few instructions long: it puts a service number, which tells the kernel which of its routines to run, into the eax register, and executes syscall.

On the other side, the kernel’s entry code moves onto a stack of its own and saves your registers. Then the kernel’s own NtReadVirtualMemory checks the request before touching anything. Both address ranges, the 4 bytes in the game and your tool’s buffer, must lie in user space, which is why ReadProcessMemory can never read kernel memory, whatever handle you hold. And the handle must carry the right the operation needs: PROCESS_VM_READ for a read, which this handle has, or PROCESS_VM_WRITE for a write, which it lacks. A handle’s rights are fixed when it is opened, and nothing done with it afterward can add one.

Only then does the kernel copy the 4 bytes into your buffer. It puts a status code in eax, here STATUS_SUCCESS, which is 0, and executes sysret, the reverse of syscall, which drops the level back to 3 and resumes your thread after its syscall. On a failure, kernelbase.dll turns the status into the error number that GetLastError reports, such as 5 for access denied. Lesson 12.6 follows each step with the values involved, including the arithmetic of the rights check.

How the kernel regains control

Section titled “How the kernel regains control”

A system call is one common way execution crosses from a user thread into the kernel. Two others are exceptions, raised by the instruction that is running (a page fault, a division by zero, the int3 breakpoint), and interrupts, signals that arrive between instructions whether or not the running program expects them.

The kernel does not interpret each ordinary game instruction. These entries bring a user thread into kernel code when work needs its authority. Windows also schedules its own kernel worker threads for work that need not begin in a game’s call. Both facts fit the same model: the kernel is code with privileged responsibilities, and the processor enforces who may run it.

The processor finds exception and interrupt handlers through the interrupt descriptor table, which the kernel fills in at boot. Each entry is chosen by a one-byte vector number. One byte holds 2⁸ = 256 values, so the table has at most 256 entries, numbered 0 to 255. The processor fixes the meaning of vectors 0 to 31: vector 3 is the breakpoint exception that the byte 0xCC, int3, raises (Lesson 2.4), vector 13 is the general-protection fault, and vector 14 is the page fault. Devices are given vectors from 32 up.

What the kernel does with its authority

Section titled “What the kernel does with its authority”

It schedules threads

Section titled “It schedules threads”

A computer has a handful of processor cores and, at any moment, hundreds or thousands of threads (Lesson 6.6 described ready, running, and waiting threads). The kernel’s scheduler decides which ready thread runs on each core. Timer interrupts are one opportunity to reconsider that choice; a thread blocking for input or a lock is another. Timer resolution and interrupt scheduling vary by Windows version, hardware, and power state, so a fixed tick interval is not a reliable description of every game session.

When a running thread stops to wait for input, a lock, or a timer, or when its turn is interrupted, the scheduler can pick another thread. Changing threads is a context switch: the kernel saves the old thread’s registers into its context, loads the new thread’s registers, and, if the new thread belongs to a different process, loads that process’s top-level page-table address into cr3. The program never sees the switch. Its registers come back exactly as they were.

Alternative: A context switch changes the bookmark and working registers for an execution path; changing processes also selects that process’s memory map.

It manages every process’s memory

Section titled “It manages every process’s memory”

Each process has its own page tables, and only the kernel writes them. Reserving an address range and committing storage are distinct operations, as Lesson 6.5 showed. Even after a page is committed, Windows may assign its physical frame only on first access. That access faults, the kernel supplies a zeroed page so old data cannot leak between processes, updates the mapping, and retries the instruction. The game normally never sees this handled fault. Lesson 6.5 looked at the result from outside, and Lesson 13.1 will examine how physical memory fits beneath that view.

Narration: A first-access page fault can be normal: the kernel supplies the page and retries the instruction. A fault does not always mean the game has crashed.

It handles interrupts

Section titled “It handles interrupts”

When a device needs attention, because a key was pressed, a disk transfer finished, or a network packet arrived, it raises an interrupt. The processor finishes its current instruction, saves where it was, enters ring 0 if it was not there already, and runs the handler for that vector. The interrupted code, kernel or user, resumes afterward as if nothing had happened. Handlers must be short, because other work on that core waits while they run; Lesson 12.7 shows how drivers split the work.

It owns devices through drivers

Section titled “It owns devices through drivers”

Ordinary user programs reach devices through operating-system interfaces rather than writing device registers directly. A driver knows a device’s register layout and command protocol, and Windows routes requests through the relevant driver stack. Lesson 12.7 follows one request down to the hardware.

It enforces security checks

Section titled “It enforces security checks”

The processor enforces privileged-instruction and page-permission checks in hardware. Windows checks handle rights and validates request ranges in the kernel, where the caller cannot simply skip the decision. The kernel also enforces the access tokens and integrity levels from Lesson 6.3, the page protections from Lesson 6.5, and the signing rules that decide which drivers may load at all (Lesson 12.7).

Recognize the subsystem in a kernel routine’s name

Section titled “Recognize the subsystem in a kernel routine’s name”

Driver documentation and debugger stacks often use short prefixes as clues to a routine’s subsystem. The table connects those names to the responsibilities above; the linked routines are reading examples, not extra lab steps.

Prefix Conceptual meaning Representative documented routine
Cm Configuration manager: registry operations CmRegisterCallbackEx registers a registry callback.
Ex Executive support: shared kernel helpers ExAllocatePool2 allocates kernel pool memory.
Hal Hardware abstraction layer: platform hardware details HalGetAdapter is an obsolete DMA-adapter example; use IoGetDmaAdapter instead.
Io I/O manager: devices and I/O requests IoCreateDevice creates a driver device object.
Ke Kernel: scheduling, synchronization, interrupt priority KeGetCurrentIrql reports the current interrupt request level.
Mm Memory manager: virtual and physical memory MmProbeAndLockPages probes and locks buffer pages.
Ob Object manager: object references and handles ObReferenceObjectByHandle checks a handle and references its object.
Po Power manager: device power transitions PoRequestPowerIrp requests a device power operation.
Tm Kernel Transaction Manager: coordinated transactions TmCommitTransaction initiates a transaction commit.
Nt Native system services NtCreateFile is a native file-service entry.
Zw The paired native-service naming convention ZwCreateFile reaches the corresponding file service.

TL;DR: A prefix identifies a family of routines; it grants no privilege. The processor’s mode, the API’s requirements, and the request’s permissions still determine what a caller can do.

Nt and Zw need one extra distinction. For system calls from user mode, their versions behave alike and treat arguments as untrusted user input. From kernel mode, Zw treats parameters as coming from a trusted kernel source; Nt uses the calling thread’s previous mode to decide how to interpret and validate them. This is a calling-context rule, not a way for a user program to gain ring 0. Microsoft’s Nt/Zw explanation describes the distinction.

Older examples need a version check. ExAllocatePool is deprecated; Microsoft’s migration guide replaces it with ExAllocatePool2 for drivers targeting Windows 10 version 2004 or later. HalGetAdapter remains listed for existing drivers, but the documented replacement is IoGetDmaAdapter. An old name in a stack can explain the subsystem without being a good choice for new code.

Why a kernel bug takes the whole machine down

Section titled “Why a kernel bug takes the whole machine down”

When user-mode code follows a bad pointer, the processor raises a page fault and the kernel handles it. The kernel checks its records, finds that nothing valid lives at that address, and turns the fault into an access-violation exception for that one process. The program’s own handler, a debugger, or Windows Error Reporting deals with it, and in the worst case one process ends. The kernel is the safety net under every user-mode program.

There is no separate part of Windows that can repair arbitrary damage to its own kernel state. A hypervisor may isolate a whole guest from the host, as Lesson 13.3 will show, but it cannot resume a guest kernel whose internal records are already corrupted. Kernel code does catch faults it expects, such as touching a user buffer that another thread may have freed; the copy behind ReadProcessMemory is written to catch exactly those. But a driver that follows a bad pointer by mistake can raise an unexpected fault inside the kernel, and kernel code and drivers share an address space and a set of data structures: the scheduler’s lists, the memory manager’s page records, and the locks that guard them. The fault may have struck halfway through updating one of those structures, with a lock still held. Windows cannot generally prove which of its own records remain sound, and carrying on could write corrupted data to disk. For an unrecoverable kernel failure, Windows stops on purpose.

That deliberate stop is a bug check, better known as the blue screen. Windows shows a stop code, such as 0x50 PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA or 0xD1 DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL, writes a crash dump of the whole machine if it can (Lesson 14.3 will capture a dump of one process), and restarts.

A bad pointer in a ring 3 program ends at most that one process. An unexpected bad pointer inside kernel code can stop the whole machine with a bug check, because kernel code and drivers share state. The interactive version needs JavaScript; the lesson text around it explains the same idea.

This is why the book keeps its labs in user mode and inside a virtual machine. The kernel trust lesson will make that design choice concrete with a read-only driver inventory. A crash in a user-mode lab ends one process, and even a bug check inside a virtual machine stops only that virtual machine (Lesson 13.3).

Why some anti-cheat runs a kernel component

Section titled “Why some anti-cheat runs a kernel component”

Anti-cheat software exists to notice when another program interferes with a game. If an anti-cheat and an interfering tool both run in user mode, both are subject to process handles, access rights, and other Windows permission checks from Chapter 11. Running at the same processor privilege does not itself grant either process access to the other. It does limit what either can establish about system-wide events and privileged components from inside its own process.

A kernel component changes that balance. Running in ring 0 lets it use documented Windows facilities that user-mode code cannot reach:

  • process and image-load notifications, so it learns about every new process and every DLL or driver as it loads, instead of scanning for them afterward;
  • handle-operation callbacks, which run while another process opens a handle to the game and may remove rights from the request. A tool that asks for read and write rights can receive a handle without them, and its ReadProcessMemory then fails at exactly the rights check described above;
  • a view of loaded drivers and system state that user-mode code cannot quietly alter.

The costs are the other half of this lesson. Anti-cheat code in the kernel has the same authority as the rest of the kernel, so its bugs become bug checks on players’ machines, and a vulnerability in it becomes a vulnerability in every machine it is installed on. It asks players to trust a game company with ring-0 code. Kernel placement also creates another boundary to protect: which drivers may load and what authority they expose. Windows uses signing rules, vulnerable driver block policies, and memory integrity to reduce that risk. Chapter 12’s driver pair explains what such code actually does and why its interface must be narrow, then examines the trust placed in a loaded driver.

References: User mode and kernel mode, process security and access rights, bug check code reference, and ObRegisterCallbacks.

Lesson 12.5

From Win32 Calls to Kernel Services

One function call can cross several layers

Section titled “One function call can cross several layers”

The course tool can now name a process, open and own a limited handle, inspect page metadata, and observe threads. Each operation was a call to a Windows API. The remaining question is where such a call goes when the tool asks the operating system to do something it cannot do directly.

A call to a Windows function such as VirtualQueryEx does not instantly jump into the deepest part of Windows. It usually passes through layers.

Alternative: Follow the call like a routed request: the public entry passes through implementation layers before a kernel service performs the privileged operation.

Use three separate ideas: contract, implementation path, and privilege transition. Win32 documents the contract application code may rely on. User-mode DLLs implement or forward that contract. A system-call instruction performs the controlled CPU transition for work that requires kernel privilege.

The boxes are software layers, not necessarily four separate processes. kernel32.dll and ntdll.dll are mapped into the same user-mode process as our program. Microsoft may change the implementation path while preserving the Win32 contract, which is why “calling a deeper layer” is usually less stable rather than more capable.

A Win32 call such as VirtualQueryEx passes down through user-mode DLLs and the system-call gate before the kernel validates it. Calling a deeper layer is usually less stable, not more capable. The interactive version needs JavaScript; the lesson text around it explains the same idea.

User mode and kernel mode are permission levels

Section titled “User mode and kernel mode are permission levels”

Most game code, application code, and Windows DLL code runs in user mode. A user-mode mistake should not be able to overwrite the kernel or another process merely by using a bad pointer.

The Windows kernel and drivers run in kernel mode, where code can manage page tables, devices, scheduling, and other system-wide resources. A bug there can affect the whole computer. That is why the course does not turn ordinary game experiments into kernel-driver experiments.

The CPU enforces this border. A system call changes privilege through a defined entry point; it is not a magic function name and it is not the same thing as calling a normal function.

This design is often described as limited direct execution. The game normally runs directly on the CPU for speed, but in user mode and within its address-space permissions. Timers and interrupts let Windows regain control for scheduling. A system call lets the game request a restricted operation through a validated entry path.

The model resolves a common confusion: Windows is not interpreting every ordinary game instruction. Most instructions execute natively. Hardware privilege, address translation, interrupts, and controlled entries provide the limits that let the OS remain in control.

Win32 is the documented application interface

Section titled “Win32 is the documented application interface”

The documented Win32 API is the part application developers are normally expected to call. Examples from this course include:

  • ReadProcessMemory for a read-only inspector with query-and-read rights;
  • VirtualQueryEx for page metadata;
  • CreateFileW for files and local named pipes;
  • CreateFileMappingW for a shared-memory object.

Microsoft can change how a supported function is implemented while keeping its documented behavior. On modern Windows, an export in kernel32.dll may forward to another DLL such as KernelBase.dll. Your source code still calls the stable Win32 name.

TL;DR: A documented Windows function can keep its contract while the DLLs and internal layers implementing it change.

A forwarded export is not a jump instruction the loader inserts. The export table entry itself can hold a string such as KERNELBASE.CreateFileW in place of a code address. When GetProcAddress resolves that entry, it reads the string, locates the named DLL, and looks up the function there instead — following another forward if that entry also happens to be one. Whoever asked for kernel32!CreateFileW never sees this redirection; they get back a usable address in KernelBase.dll either way, which is exactly why Microsoft can move an implementation between DLLs across Windows versions without breaking the caller’s import:

Native APIs sit closer to the system call

Section titled “Native APIs sit closer to the system call”

ntdll.dll exposes many functions whose names begin with Nt, such as NtQueryVirtualMemory. Some native functions are documented for limited uses and many are not stable application contracts.

For ordinary tools, prefer documented interfaces:

“Closer to the kernel” does not mean “better for normal application code.”

Calling an undocumented entry point or copying a system-call number from one Windows build can make a tool fragile. Numbers and internal structures can change. The course resolves one native export so you can see the layer, but it deliberately does not call it or build a direct-syscall bypass.

DLL exports are names offered to other code

Section titled “DLL exports are names offered to other code”

A DLL can publish an export table. Each exported name maps to an entry that the loader can resolve. GetProcAddress asks a loaded module for one of those exports.

The returned address is a virtual address in the current process. Address Space Layout Randomization, or ASLR, means the same DLL can be mapped at a different base address in another process or after a reboot. Store the name or an RVA when that is the stable identity; do not paste a displayed absolute address into tomorrow’s program.

Narration: A printed export address belongs to this process and mapping. Reusing its name or verified relative location avoids assuming tomorrow’s mapping uses the same base.

Build the address inspector

Section titled “Build the address inspector”

The lab gets handles to DLLs already loaded in its own process, resolves three names, and prints their process-local addresses. It never opens a game process and never calls the native function:

Complete lab source: api_layers.rs

api_layers.rs

windows-labs/src/bin/ · Rust, 58 lines

View on GitHub ↗

Why GetModuleHandleW instead of LoadLibraryW?

Section titled “Why GetModuleHandleW instead of LoadLibraryW?”

Both DLLs are already present in a normal Windows console process. GetModuleHandleW borrows their existing module handles; it does not request another load or add a loader reference that we would later need to release.

Why does GetProcAddress use an ASCII name?

Section titled “Why does GetProcAddress use an ASCII name?”

PE export names are byte strings. The s! macro creates a terminated static PCSTR. DLL file names use Windows wide strings, so GetModuleHandleW receives values from the w! macro instead.

This original attempt mixes byte strings and wide strings. It is intentionally a non-compiling example: the Windows bindings reject the wrong parameter types before any call runs.

Use w! for the wide DLL filename and s! for the byte-encoded export name. Both strings are static and terminated; the DLL handle is borrowed for the lookup.

In this version, FARPROC already means an optional generic function pointer. ok_or_else removes that Option wrapper; the helper returns its address as usize for display. It does not call that pointer as VirtualQueryEx. The version-pinned type and lookup signature explain this return-type choice.

Improved code

Optional: practise matching the full API names, module argument and address type to their jobs.

Show the diff

Takeaway: the API’s string type determines the encoding, even when both arguments look like ordinary names.

The types make the two encodings visible instead of silently mixing them.

Read the Windows signature before translating it

Section titled “Read the Windows signature before translating it”

Microsoft’s C documentation uses names such as DWORD, BOOL, and HANDLE to describe the API’s binary contract. Match that contract rather than choosing a Rust type just because its name sounds similar:

Windows spelling What it means at the boundary Rust reading rule
DWORD Unsigned 32-bit integer, even in a 64-bit process Usually u32; it does not grow into usize.
BOOL Signed 32-bit integer Boolean value Raw i32, or the binding’s projected type or result; Rust bool has a different representation. For Boolean truth, test nonzero rather than equality to 1.
HANDLE Opaque, pointer-sized object handle Use the binding’s handle type; it is not a Rust reference that you may dereference.

These distinctions come from Windows coding conventions and Windows data types. Read each function’s return-value section too: its success and failure rules can be more specific than its return type.

The lab’s string-width mistake is one instance of a broader convention. In paired string APIs, W accepts UTF-16 code units and A accepts 8-bit text in the API’s ANSI encoding; A is not a promise of ASCII or UTF-8. C headers may select an unsuffixed name using the UNICODE macro. Calling the explicit W function keeps the choice visible in Rust. See Working with Strings.

The ABI, or application binary interface, also specifies how arguments and results pass between caller and callee. WINAPI and CALLBACK in C signatures mark a calling convention, not an access right. Generated bindings supply the matching declarations. For a callback declared with that convention, match its exact signature and Rust’s extern "system" ABI: its underlying convention depends on the target, including stdcall on 32-bit Windows for non-variadic functions.

TL;DR: A handle’s size does not tell you who owns it. Check the API that produced it and its documented release rule; this lab’s borrowed module handle must not be released with FreeLibrary.

The GetModuleHandleW contract is the ownership rule behind that note. Likewise, a string pointer must stay valid for as long as the receiving API uses it; a pointer wrapper alone does not own its storage.

Which windows-rs crate does what?

Section titled “Which windows-rs crate does what?”

The crate names describe different jobs in the Rust bindings. They do not change which Windows layer runs a call or what the caller may access.

Crate Role
windows Generated projected APIs for Win32, COM, and WinRT, with typed values and conversions. This is the lab’s API crate.
windows-sys Raw Windows ABI declarations; the caller manages pointer contracts, ownership, and error translation.
windows-core Shared COM and WinRT interface types, traits, and projection support.
windows-strings Windows string representations, including owning strings and borrowed pointer wrappers.
windows-result Windows status and error types, including HRESULT and Result.

The generation tools have separate jobs: windows-bindgen turns Windows metadata into Rust bindings; windows-metadata reads and writes that metadata; windows-clang extracts C/C++ header declarations using libclang. The lab consumes pre-generated bindings. Add support or generation crates only when your own task needs them; many support types are already re-exported by the API crate.

One similarly named crate, windows-reference, boxes a value for a WinRT signature that requires IReference<T>. That is a Windows interface object, distinct from ordinary Rust borrowing with &T. The address inspector needs no such boxed value.

Run it and compare two launches

Section titled “Run it and compare two launches”
Windows VM

The program prints exported function names beside their addresses in this process. Its first run establishes a local observation; the second run tests whether those addresses are safe to treat as permanent identifiers.

Run it again after restarting the virtual machine and compare the addresses. A difference is expected. The names and behavior are the meaningful pieces.

Then use module_inventory against wesnoth.exe, ac_client.exe, or Quake3-UrT.exe. You are looking at two sides of the same loader idea:

  • module_inventory shows which DLL images the game loaded;
  • api_layers shows how one process asks a loaded DLL for an exported name.

The complete program is api_layers.rs.

References: libraries and native-system-service entry points, using Nt and Zw routines, GetModuleHandleW, and GetProcAddress.

Lesson 12.6

System Calls and Privilege Checks

Lesson 12.4 showed the processor keeping user-mode code away from the kernel and drew one ReadProcessMemory call crossing into the kernel and back. This lesson opens both up. It reads the bits the processor actually checks, then follows that one call a layer at a time, with every value the kernel compares along the way.

The current level is two bits of a register

Section titled “The current level is two bits of a register”

The processor keeps the current privilege level in the lowest two bits of the cs register, which tells the processor which code segment it is running. Two bits can hold 2 × 2 = 4 patterns, 00, 01, 10, and 11, which is exactly why there are four rings.

Open any 64-bit program in x64dbg and the register panel shows cs as 0033:

0x33 is 3 × 16 + 3 = 51. Each hex digit stands for four bits, so 0x33 is 0011 0011. Its lowest two bits are 11, which is 2 + 1 = 3: ring 3, user mode. The kernel’s own code segment is 0x10, which is 0001 0000; its lowest two bits are 00, ring 0.

A program cannot promote itself by loading 0x10 into cs. The processor refuses any change of code segment that would raise the privilege level, except through a few entry points that the kernel prepared in advance. The most important of them is the syscall instruction, and the rest of this lesson follows one trip through it.

One bit marks a page as the kernel’s

Section titled “One bit marks a page as the kernel’s”

Lesson 12.4 said that a page-table entry’s user/supervisor bit, bit 2, decides whether ring 3 may touch the page. An entry combines the address of a physical page with flags describing that mapping. For the ordinary 4 KiB pages used here, the page address is aligned on a 4,096-byte boundary, leaving the low twelve bits available for flags. Chapter 12’s address-translation lesson will follow a complete walk; here we need only the permission flags in the lowest byte:

0x67 is 6 × 16 + 7 = 103, and 103 = 64 + 32 + 4 + 2 + 1, so bits 6, 5, 2, 1, and 0 are set. Bit 0 says the page is present, bit 1 that it may be written, and bit 2 that ring 3 may use it. The processor itself sets bit 5, accessed, the first time the page is used, and bit 6, dirty, the first time it is written. Bits 3, 4, and 7 control caching and are 0 here.

A page that holds kernel data looks almost the same:

0x67 − 0x63 = 4, and 4 = 2², so exactly one bit differs between these two example leaf entries: bit 2. A kernel page can be present, writable, and recently used, and still refuse access from ring 3. In a real page-table walk, the processor also considers permissions in the entries at higher levels; a single leaf byte is a teaching example, not a complete access decision.

The same call, one layer at a time

Section titled “The same call, one layer at a time”

Take a read like the ones in Lesson 6.3: a handle to the game opened with only query and read rights, and a request for 4 bytes at address 0x0050_1000. Lesson 12.4 drew the whole round trip as one sequence diagram, from your tool through kernel32.dll, kernelbase.dll, and ntdll.dll to the processor and the kernel, and back. This section follows that diagram one participant at a time.

Inside your process

Section titled “Inside your process”

ReadProcessMemory in kernel32.dll forwards to kernelbase.dll (Lesson 12.5), which calls NtReadVirtualMemory in ntdll.dll with the same arguments. The ntdll function is a stub: a few instructions whose only job is to make the system call. On 64-bit Windows its core is four instructions:

The first line exists because of the first thing syscall does. The Windows x64 calling convention passes a function’s first argument in rcx, but syscall overwrites rcx with the return address, so the stub moves the argument to r10 first, and the kernel knows to look for it there.

Narration: The system-call instruction overwrites rcx, so the stub preserves the first argument in r10. Missing that move would change what the kernel receives.

The number in eax is a system service number, an index into the kernel’s table of routines. The numbers are internal to Windows and change between builds, which is why this book never copies one into a program. In a debugger the stub also shows a test and a jump to an older entry instruction, int 2Eh, that some configurations use; either way, the processor arrives at an address the kernel chose.

Crossing over

Section titled “Crossing over”

The kernel’s entry code assumes that everything user mode handed it could be hostile. It switches from the program’s stack to a kernel stack that belongs to the thread, because the program’s stack pointer could point anywhere.
